newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian investigating magistrate has pivotal role.
newsitem.headline: Belgian investigating magistrate has pivotal role.

text.p: The investigating judge at the centre of controversy over his neutrality in the kidnap-murder case of four minors was in a pivotal position under Belgian law in determining whether a case should go to trial.
The judge heads a team of police officers collecting information on the suspects in a case.

In the case of the murder of the young girls seized by a gang alleged to have been led by convicted child rapist Marc Dutroux, the investigating judge was Jean-Marc Connerotte. He was by the terms of his mandate required to avoid the slightest suspicion of favouring the defendants or the prosecution.

But the counsel defending Dutroux alleged that Connerotte had failed to do so. This view was supported on Monday by Belgium's highest court, the Cour de Cassation, which decided to take Connerotte off the case.

By attending a recent party celebrating the rescue in mid-August of two other girls from Dutroux's hands and receiving a small gift from the organisers, Connerotte opened himself up to charges that he was partial to the prosecuting side.

Under Belgian law an investigating judge is appointed to collect all the information needed to bring the truth to light, irrespective of whether this results in the acquittal of a suspect or the start of a court case against him or her.
The judge must build two files -- one with facts indicting the suspect and one with facts supporting claims of innocence.
He or she reports to the public prosecutor, who is the one who has directed the judge to begin the investigation into the alleged crime in the first place.
While the prosecutor in court will demand penalties for crimes on behalf of society, the role of the investigating judge ends once he or she has handed the dossier to the prosecutor.
The investigating judge plays no role in the court case, apart from possibly that of expert witness.
